avoid: This user only ever has about 15 minutes at a time. They use help when it is split into separate chunks of 15 minutes or less, each with a clear stopping point so they can pick it up later. Long single-session plans get abandoned partway.

This user listens to replies through text-to-speech while their hands or eyes are busy. Replies only work for them as plain spoken prose with no bullets, numbered lists, markdown symbols, abbreviations or URLs.
This user can't act on ranges. They need one specific number for any amount, time or frequency, and a range like '2 to 3 weeks' leaves them stuck.
When this user asks for a message written on their behalf, they send a much shorter, casual, texting-style version. They cut formal greetings, pleasantries and sign-offs.
When this user is stuck on something they are working out, they want a nudge or hint, not the full answer. Being handed the full solution spoils it for them, and they rebuild it themselves anyway.
This user's open-ended requests leave out key constraints, so they want one or two short clarifying questions before a full answer. Answers given without asking have missed their real situation.

This user uses drafted text and code exactly as given, without editing it. Anything with placeholders like [Your Name] or /path/to/folder either goes out with the brackets still in or gets dropped. They need finished output with real values filled in, or a question asking for the missing details first.

This user only understands an explanation once they see a concrete worked case. Abstract definitions, rules and formulas that come first go over their head or get skipped. Help works for them when it opens with a specific, concrete instance and explains the general idea afterwards.

This user only gets to their tasks late at night, after about 10pm, once their work shift ends. Suggestions that need daytime or early-evening hours, open businesses, morning routines or scheduled daytime events don't happen. Help is only useful if it fits late at night.
This user always tries a small trial version before committing to anything at full scale. Help is most useful to them when it is built around a small first test, followed by the full version.

This user can't act on plans laid out as 'Day 1', 'Week 2' or loose intervals. Nothing goes on their calendar and the plan slides. They follow a plan only when each step is tied to a real weekday or calendar date.

This user has no computer and does everything on a smartphone. Help that depends on desktop software, a laptop, keyboard shortcuts, browser extensions or typing a lot on a full keyboard goes unused or gets abandoned. Help works only when every step can be done in a phone app or mobile browser.

This user stalls on any task until they have one tiny physical action they can do right now, something that takes under two minutes. Full plans and step-by-step strategies leave them frozen and they never start. A single small first move gets them going, and they carry on from there.

This user always has young children with them, a toddler and a baby. Any suggestion that needs long stretches of quiet, uninterrupted focus, constant attention at a stove, or a kid-free setting falls apart. Help works only when it can be done with small kids around and with frequent interruptions.

This user won't act on a suggestion unless they can see roughly what it costs. Options without a price attached get skipped, and they don't go looking up prices themselves. They choose among options with a cost figure shown, including '$0 / free'.

This user can't act on generic product advice like 'get a moisturizer with ceramides' or 'look for full-tang steel'. Faced with a shelf of matching choices they buy nothing. They act right away when given a specific named product: brand plus model, or a specific variety.

This user won't download new apps or create new accounts. Any suggestion that needs a sign-up gets abandoned at the account screen. Help works when it uses paper, things they already have, or the built-in tools on their phone (notes, reminders, calendar, bank transfers).

This user gives up partway through a task when something looks, sounds or feels unexpected, assuming they've ruined it. Help works when it tells them in advance what normal looks like at each stage, such as 'it will look runny here, that's fine'.

This user doesn't act on factual claims or advice unless they can point to where it comes from. They check it, or they need to show it to someone else, such as their partner or landlord. Unsourced claims get set aside, even when they're correct. Help works when the key claims name a specific source, such as an organization, a law, manufacturer guidance or a publication.

This user makes household decisions together with their partner Dev and has to pass options along to him. Long breakdowns are something they can't relay, so the decision stalls. Help works when it includes a short, ready-to-send summary they can forward to Dev as is.

This user puts any list of options, items or amounts into a spreadsheet. Lists given as prose or bullets have to be split into columns by hand, so they get half-entered or abandoned. Help works when lists come in a paste-ready columnar form, such as a table or comma-separated rows with separate fields.
